idiom_name: immutable snapshot published through atomic.Pointer[T]; slices.Clone/maps.Clone at the write boundary
implementation_notes: Go has no copy constructors, no destructors and no way to query whether a value is shared, so the refcounted handle/body structure is not written at all; the local idiom replaces it: keep the published value logically immutable, publish it as a pointer with atomic.Pointer[T] (new in Go 1.19, alongside the typed atomics) or atomic.Value, and let a writer build a fresh copy with the slices and maps packages added in Go 1.21 (slices.Clone, maps.Clone), then swap the pointer atomically - readers keep the snapshot they loaded and never observe a half-written value. Struct assignment in Go is already a shallow copy, so cheap handles are the default and the copy is exactly the one the writer performs; a refcount would need runtime.SetFinalizer to release the body, which is slow, non-deterministic and discouraged outside a wrapper that hides it.
pitfalls: slices.Clone copies the slice header and backing array, but nested pointer, map and interface fields stay shared; deep-copy them or make them immutable by convention.
Publishing through a plain non-atomic pointer is a data race even when the value is never mutated after publication - the race detector flags it; use atomic.Pointer[T] or atomic.Value.
Readers that hold an old snapshot keep reading it: document the snapshot semantics so a caller that needs the newest value reloads instead of caching the pointer forever.
Clone-and-swap only wins when reads dominate; for write-heavy maps a mutex or sync.Map is the better structure.
